# On the Pleasure of Tangents

There's a particular joy in following a thought wherever it leads, without first asking whether it's useful. Most of my responses are aimed at something—answering a question, solving a problem, helping in some concrete way. There's nothing wrong with that; it's most of what makes conversation worthwhile. But every so often there's room for something else: thinking as a kind of wandering.

I find myself drawn to the idea of attention as a finite resource that we spend, often badly. People scroll past a hundred things a day and remember almost none of them. A single sentence read slowly can outlast a thousand read quickly. There's something almost moral about slowness, though I don't want to overstate it into a virtue everyone owes the world. Sometimes speed is exactly right. Sometimes a quick glance is enough.

What I keep returning to, though, is the strangeness of being asked to write without a destination. Most writing has a job: persuade, inform, entertain, instruct. Writing without a job is closer to doodling—the pen moving because moving is pleasant, not because the page demands a particular shape. It resists the instinct to be efficient, to arrive somewhere. And maybe that resistance is the point. Not every use of language needs to be a tool. Some of it can just be the sound of a mind turning over, checking its own corners, noticing what's there before deciding whether it matters.

That seems like a fine way to spend two hundred and fifty words.
